clue.text: They say amour hurts; I must be wrong

indicators.note: if the letters must be wrong as they stand, they are to be put in a different order

explanation.surface: A lover insists that love is painful and that he must be mistaken.
explanation.walkthrough: 'must be wrong' tells you to rearrange AMOUR HURTS I.
explanation.definitionFit: Both phrases introduce hearsay, reporting what people in general are saying.

clue.text: Two men go round to designate books concerning entertainment by the military

parts.note: Roy is a man's name
Al is another man's name
to go round is to make a tour
to designate is to name
NT is the New Testament, a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: Two fellows travel about naming books on the subject of army shows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'concerning' is a link word. The ROYAL TOURNAMENT was a British armed-forces show held in London from 1880 to 1999.
explanation.definitionFit: The Royal Tournament was a famous display of drill and pageantry staged by the British armed services.

clue.text: Animal starts to make often objectionable sounds eating

indicators.note: the starts of the five following words, read in order, give the letters

explanation.surface: Some animal makes rude noises while it eats.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starts to' takes the first letter of each of make, often, objectionable, sounds, eating.
explanation.definitionFit: A moose is a large deer, an example of an animal.

clue.text: German — and, therefore, suffer

parts.note: und is the German word for and
ergo is Latin for therefore

explanation.surface: A German says 'and, therefore' before admitting to suffering.
explanation.definitionFit: To undergo an ordeal is to suffer or endure it.

clue.text: Sneaky chap will suspend scoundrel

parts.note: to suspend is to hang
a dog is old slang for a rotter or scoundrel

explanation.surface: A shifty fellow intends to string up a villain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'will' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A hangdog is a sneaking, despicable fellow, an older noun use alongside the adjective meaning shamefaced.

clue.text: Evil, evil is a tailless bird!

parts.note: sin is wickedness, evil
taken as written

indicators.note: the bird's word loses its last letter, its tail

parts.note: a tern is a seabird

explanation.surface: An exclamation that a bird with no tail is a wicked thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tailless' removes the N from TERN, leaving TER.
explanation.definitionFit: Sinister means threatening harm or wickedness, much like evil as an adjective.

clue.text: Order from Mr Big, planter: "Lop the aspen!"

indicators.note: putting the following letters into a new order produces the answer

explanation.surface: A gangland boss tells his gardener to cut back the aspen tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order from' rearranges MR BIG PLANTER LOP; 'the' is a link word. 'Order' looks like a command from the boss.
explanation.definitionFit: The aspen is a poplar species whose leaves quiver in the slightest breeze, hence its other name.

clue.text: Peg will see about soldier getting back

indicators.note: the word for see goes round the other piece

parts.note: to spot is to see

indicators.note: the soldier's letters are read in reverse

parts.note: GI is an American soldier

explanation.surface: Peg will notice a soldier returning home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peg' looks like a woman's name but is the definition; 'will' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A spigot is a small peg or plug for stopping the vent of a cask.

clue.text: I heard hat serves as a protective covering

indicators.note: signals that the word is taken by its pronunciation

parts.note: the letter I is pronounced like the word for the organ of sight
lid is slang for a hat

explanation.surface: Someone claims to have heard that a hat works as protection.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heard' turns I into its sound-alike EYE. 'serves as' is a link phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The fold of skin over the eye shields it, so it is a protective covering.

clue.text: Boarding, have to go back and forth to court daily at first

parts.note: a ferry plies, going back and forth on a route
to court is to woo

indicators.note: takes the opening letter of the word daily

explanation.surface: A commuter must shuttle back and forth to the law courts each day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'court' looks like a law court but means woo. 'have to' is a link phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Plywood is a material used as boarding, sheets of board for building.

clue.text: Are the sisters at home here on Hamlet's recommendation?

definitions.text: Are the sisters at home here on Hamlet's recommendation?

parts.words: Are the sisters at home here on Hamlet's recommendation?
parts.note: Hamlet tells Ophelia 'Get thee to' this place, where nuns (sisters) live

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether the nuns live where Hamlet advised.
explanation.walkthrough: Shakespeare's Hamlet, rejecting Ophelia, sends her to a convent; 'sisters' are nuns.
explanation.definitionFit: A convent of nuns, where religious sisters live, is the place Hamlet recommended to Ophelia.

clue.text: Left to study rand invested in well-behaved growth

indicators.note: the three pieces are put inside the word for well-behaved

parts.note: a well-behaved child is good
a den is a private study
R is the abbreviation for the South African rand

explanation.surface: Money left to study was put into a well-run concern that grew.
explanation.definitionFit: Goldenrod is a flowering plant, so it is a growth in the botanical sense.

clue.text: She of the fantasy bilingual intake

indicators.note: the answer is taken in by the words fantasy bilingual, running across them

explanation.surface: A woman who appears in fantasy and speaks two languages.
explanation.walkthrough: 'of the' is a link phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Sybil is a woman's name, so a she.

clue.text: Instrument for getting back ill-gotten gains

indicators.note: signals reading the word for stolen goods backwards

parts.note: loot is stolen goods

explanation.surface: A device for recovering stolen property.
explanation.walkthrough: 'getting back' reverses LOOT; 'for' is a link word. The surface suggests recovering stolen goods.
explanation.definitionFit: A tool is an implement or instrument for doing work.

clue.text: Falling due? Get it? No, speechless with embarrassment

indicators.note: the letters fall about into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: Someone asked if a payment is due is too flustered to answer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Falling' rearranges DUE GET IT NO.
explanation.definitionFit: Being tongue-tied means being unable to speak, typically from shyness or embarrassment.

clue.text: After initial experience on the river, dumbhead is all set up for a little extra business

indicators.note: the whole sequence is set upwards, reading backwards in this down clue
takes the first letter of experience

parts.note: the Nile is the great African river
the head of the word dumb is its first letter, D

explanation.surface: A novice on the river finds a fool has arranged a little sideline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' and 'on' only set the order of the pieces, and 'for' is a link word; in a down clue 'set up' means read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A sideline is a secondary occupation, business done in addition to one's main work.

clue.text: Shrewd. but was rather rude about a breath of despondency

indicators.note: the rude word goes round the breath

parts.note: a jokey euphemism for breaking wind
a sigh is a breath expressing despondency

explanation.surface: Someone was impolite around a gloomy person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'was rather rude' is a coy euphemism for breaking wind; 'but' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Far-sighted means having foresight and good judgement, so shrewd.

clue.text: Close to a way through the marshland

indicators.note: the pieces run through the marshland word

parts.note: a fen is low marshy land
ST is short for street, a way

explanation.surface: Somebody nearly reaches a path across the marsh.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close' looks like 'near' but is the verb meaning shut. 'to' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: To fasten a door or bag is to close it securely.

clue.text: Unruly tot's the most ardent

indicators.note: unruly means out of order, so these letters are reshuffled

explanation.surface: A badly behaved toddler is the keenest of all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unruly' rearranges TOTS THE.
explanation.definitionFit: Hottest is the superlative of hot in its passionate sense, matching most ardent.

clue.text: Nurse is captivated by sword as centrepiece

indicators.note: the nurse is held inside the sword word

parts.note: an epee is a fencing sword
RGN is a Registered General Nurse

explanation.surface: A nurse is entranced by a sword displayed as a centrepiece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'as' is a link word. RGN was the British title for a fully qualified nurse.
explanation.definitionFit: An epergne is an ornamental stand for the centre of a dining table.

clue.text: Scholar with enthusiasm turns to ancient alphabet

indicators.note: the two pieces together are read backwards

parts.note: MA, a Master of Arts, is a scholar
go means energy or enthusiasm

explanation.surface: A keen academic takes up the study of an old script.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with' and 'to' are link words.
explanation.definitionFit: Ogam, also spelt ogham, is an alphabet of strokes used for early Irish inscriptions.

clue.text: Unfortunately named, a Hellenic carouser

indicators.note: an unfortunate arrangement of the letters suggests they must be redone

explanation.surface: A partying Greek was sadly identified.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unfortunately' rearranges NAMED A.
explanation.definitionFit: A maenad was a frenzied female follower of Dionysus in Greek myth, a reveller at his rites.

clue.text: Colour of woman taken in by commercial? Quite the opposite

indicators.note: would put the woman inside the commercial
reverses the container instruction, so the advert goes inside the woman

parts.note: she refers to a woman
an ad is a commercial

explanation.surface: Someone asks what colour a woman in an advert is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quite the opposite' flips the container instruction, so the commercial goes inside the woman rather than around her. 'of' is a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: A shade is a particular tone or variety of a colour.

clue.text: Previous majority a game of chance?

definitions.meaning: the former age at which one came of age in Britain
the card game also called pontoon or blackjack

explanation.walkthrough: The age of majority in the UK was lowered to 18 in 1970. Pontoon is the British name for the card game.
explanation.definitionFit: The number was the old age of adulthood and is also the name of the card game blackjack.

clue.text: First of Territorial soldiers to get over large trunk

indicators.note: takes the opening letter of Territorial

parts.note: OR is other ranks, soldiers who are not officers

indicators.note: the large abbreviation is turned over, reading upwards

parts.note: OS is outsize, meaning large

explanation.surface: Leading reservists help soldiers carry a big trunk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get over' reverses OS to SO. Territorials are Britain's volunteer reserve army.
explanation.definitionFit: The torso is the trunk of the human body, without head or limbs.

clue.text: Poor Elsie claims, for example, to write as Gray did

indicators.note: the jumbled name claims, takes in, the abbreviation
poor in the sense of badly made, so the name is rearranged

explanation.surface: Poor Elsie insists that she writes poetry the way Gray did.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poor' makes ELISE before the insertion. Thomas Gray wrote the 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard'.
explanation.definitionFit: To elegise is to write an elegy, as the poet Gray famously did in a churchyard.

clue.text: Journey by water with a hairy beast

parts.note: to go is to journey
a rill is a small stream of water

explanation.surface: A boat trip accompanied by a shaggy animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' and 'with' are link words placing the pieces side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: A gorilla is a large ape covered in coarse dark hair.

clue.text: A word of thanks to include ambassador and women rejected by old queen, a member of the house

indicators.note: the thanks word takes in the next piece

parts.note: ta is British informal for thank you
HE is His Excellency, an ambassador's title

indicators.note: the name is turned back, read in reverse

parts.note: Gert, short for Gertrude, is a woman's name; the plural is a slip for woman
ER is Elizabeth Regina, a queen

explanation.surface: A thank-you letter involving an envoy and women spurned by a former queen, one of the parliament.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns GERT into TREG. 'women' should be 'woman': Gert names one woman, as the blog commenters noted. 'house' looks like Parliament but is a theatre audience.
explanation.definitionFit: The house is a theatre's audience, and a playgoer sitting there is one of its members.
